entries.title: Papaya Leaf (Pawpaw)
entries.subtitle: Carica papaya
entries.tip: Rich in papain enzymes; crushed green fruit or leaf sap has long been used to tenderize meat and soothe stings.
entries.summary: Hollow-stemmed tropical tree crowned with giant deeply lobed leaves and clusters of sweet golden fruit.
entries.notes:
Traditional Bush Use: Bitter infusions of young papaya leaf are used regionally for digestion and recovery support, while the milky latex from unripe fruit soothes insect bites and tenderizes tough cuts.

Safety: Avoid concentrated leaf decoctions during pregnancy.
entries.identification: Unbranched straight trunk marked with leaf scars, topped by a rosette of huge 7-lobed palmate leaves.
entries.bestMix: Steep a small piece of leaf with Ginger Root and honey to balance its bitterness.

entries.title: Passionfruit Leaf & Vine
entries.subtitle: Passiflora edulis
entries.tip: Steeping 2–3 dried passionfruit leaves makes a calming evening tea for restful sleep.
entries.summary: Vigorous climbing vine with intricate purple-and-white flowers, tart aromatic fruit, and calming leaves.
entries.notes:
Traditional Bush Use: Leaves and young tendrils are steeped as a gentle nervine tea to ease restlessness, tension, and support sleep.

Field Note: Watch for the dramatic fringed corona of the flower, which attracts carpenter bees along sunny trail borders.
entries.identification: Climbing vine with coiled tendrils, glossy 3-lobed leaves, and ornate white-and-purple radial flowers.
entries.bestMix: Pairs well with Vervine or Soursop leaf for an evening wind-down tea.

entries.title: Bird Vine (Caribbean Mistletoe)
entries.subtitle: Phoradendron spp.
entries.tip: Spread from tree to tree by birds eating its sticky berries; traditionally steeped in small amounts for circulation.
entries.summary: A semi-parasitic evergreen cluster growing high on citrus, mango, and forest tree branches.
entries.notes:
Traditional Bush Use: Small amounts of the leathery leaves are traditionally simmered by herbalists for blood pressure and circulation support.

Ecology: Birds wipe the sticky seeds onto high branches, where the plant taps into the host tree's sap while still photosynthesizing.
entries.identification: Rounded clumps of thick, yellowish-green opposite leaves perched directly on tree limbs, with tiny clustered berries.
entries.bestMix: Used sparingly with Soursop leaf or Breadfruit leaf; consult a knowledgeable guide.

entries.title: Castor Oil Leaf (Palma Christi)
entries.subtitle: Ricinus communis
entries.tip: EXTERNAL USE ONLY: Warmed leaves are applied as a poultice for joint aches — seeds are deadly toxic if eaten.
entries.summary: Broad, star-shaped palmate leaves prized externally as a warm poultice; seeds contain potent ricin and must never be ingested.
entries.notes:
Safety Warning: Do NOT eat any part of this plant. The mottled seeds contain ricin, a dangerous toxin.

Traditional External Use: Elders lightly warm the large leaves over a flame or rub them with coconut oil and wrap them around sore knees, sprains, or headaches.
entries.identification: Tall soft-wooded shrub with large glossy, deeply lobed star-shaped leaves (7–9 lobes) and spiny red-green seed capsules.
entries.bestMix: External leaf poultice only (never brew as a tea).

entries.title: Tamarind Leaf & Pod
entries.subtitle: Tamarindus indica
entries.tip: Young tamarind leaves boiled in water make a classic Caribbean soothing wash and fever bath.
entries.summary: Feathery compound leaves and tangy brown seed pods from one of St. Kitts' most iconic shade trees.
entries.notes:
Traditional Bush Use: Young leaves are steeped for mild fevers and sore throats, or boiled into a soothing bath for prickly heat and skin irritation. The tart pulp is rich in natural electrolytes and gentle fiber.

Ecology: Thrives in sunny, dry coastal lowlands and historic estate yards.
entries.identification: Large spreading tree with airy, pinnate leaves (10–20 pairs of small leaflets) and curved, brittle cinnamon-brown pods.
entries.bestMix: Steep young leaves with a touch of ginger or lime peel.

entries.title: Sweet Broom (Licorice Weed)
entries.subtitle: Scoparia dulcis
entries.tip: Locals tie bundled stems into yard brooms and steep the whole herb as a mild cooling tea.
entries.summary: A slender, branching tropical herb with tiny white four-petaled flowers and a faintly sweet, cooling taste.
entries.notes:
Traditional Bush Use: Steeped as a cooling bush tea for mild fevers, coughs, and digestive discomfort across St. Kitts and Nevis.

Field Note: Also called 'Sweet Broom' because its tough, wiry stems were historically tied together for sweeping yards.
entries.identification: Small erect herb (1–2 ft) with opposite serrated leaves and tiny 4-petaled white flowers along upper stems.
entries.bestMix: Pairs well with Fever Grass (Lemongrass) or Vervine for a light cooling tea.
